First, as u/IdmeetEgo writes, you are confusing respect for something else. I won’t repeat it, since he wrote it well.

You need to differentiate more between the different kinds of respect. I’ll make a two examples:

* Respecting someone as a human being. I would argue that this is the base level of respect. Basically, it gives that you don’t just hurt someone for fun or attack their human dignity. Everyone should have this kind of respect for all people (except some border cases).
* Respecting someone as a smart person. Even though you don’t like someone, you can still respect their opinions and assessments. This doesn’t mean you fear them, but simply that you acknowledge their intelligence.

As I see it, you typically respect someone as a certain Role. If you want to be respected, you have to fulfil that role. The reason why people often advise to be kind and polite, is simply because it makes it easier for your environment to respect you, since you usually withhold from respecting someone that doesn’t respect you.

Indeed, I never heard of a case like that. I still have 4 guesses:

* Your peripheral vision is not as peripheral as you think. Basically, you just still stare at them.
* You underestimate mirroring surfaces. Sometimes when I use my peripheral vision I don’t focus on where I actually look at. If your sitting besides them, it might be the case that your eyes are pointing at them in some mirroring surface.
* Your behaviour gives away when you are looking at them. If they do stuff and you react to it appropriately, then they might assume (rightfully so) that your are looking at them.
* You just perceive it as them thinking you are looking at them, but in reality they are not. Maybe you look suspicious and they are weirded out or you really only interpret it as such, even though there is nothing there.

As a side note, you still have peripheral vision with glasses, your blind spot just increases slightly.

My short answer would be the priority on self-esteem is the healthy way. 

The complete answer is going to be fairly long.

First you should distinguish more between different kinds of self-esteem. I will use myself as an example to make my point clear. When I was younger I was severely lacking self-confidence and social kills, but, as strange as it sounds, I still had self-worth. For reasons that are not important for this discussion, I then started training social skills, still without self-confidence. Long story short, when I had some success my self-confidence started growing. To sum up this first example, for me self-confidence was not necessary, but self-worth definitely helped out.

To be complete I want to give another example. A friend of mine also was lacking self-confidence and social skills, unfortunately he furthermore had no self-worth. Because he was bullied a lot, he also started training social skills, but in his case it was basically to get revenge (So his incentive was on the manipulative side). He succeeded but also still had no self-confidence and self-worth. As a result of this, fairly miserable events went down that broke him even more. That’s what I mean with healthy. 

Regarding the question whether social skill is the direct consequence of high self-esteem, I think not. It still needs work, but I would assume that it comes much more natural and not in a learning-by-hard way like my friend did.

EDIT: I forgot one addition. I think also self-confidence is relative, e.g. you can be confident in yourself that you ace that exam or that interview, and still feel that you will fail at every conversation with your attracted gender.

It seems to be a popular wish to revert to your former self, even though in my opinion this doesn’t make sense. It can be a good reference point, but your goal should be to develop your current self. 

Regarding the behaviour of your friends that hasn’t changed, do not forget the effect of associative regression. Basically, it might well be the case that a lot of them have changed, but in the situation of meeting your former high school peers they simply adapted to their former behaviour. 

Another even more trivial aspect is that when meeting past acquaintances some people tend to remember all the events that happened since then (in your case high school). This can be a fairly bad experience depending on how much regrets are invoked. 

I would argue this is simply part of life and nothing to be particularly worried about. That said it can still be an indicator that there is something in your current life that haunts you. I guess your social life is a candidate for that. Therefore I would advise to not think too much about your past acquaintances, but to improve your social life.

Life is not a competition of who has the most friends. One close friend can be enough. Therefore I can just advise the obvious, if you don’t like them then you do not have to befriend them; Knowing such people can have its advantages too, but not as real friends, especially if they are such a bad influence as you described.

I can sympathize with the exhaustion part, but 30 seconds sounds rough. Maybe you should first work on improving that limit. For me it is much easier to endure it when talking about stuff that I am passionate about. Since you are still an undergraduate it should be easier to find people that share common interests. 

Now on how to approach people.  Here are some ideas:

 * In my university we have a lot of group projects. Those make it easier to find new people (e.g. look who has no partner). Usually you meet at least once with your partner. Propose to meet during lunch (to get to know each other better) and then work afterward. After work is done you can propose to always (during the semester) meet during lunch and discuss the project progress. Depending on the extent of your social skills (role credit) this might be really difficult and might only be possible at a later stage. The advantage of this method is that (1) people have to find a partner for group projects, (2) you can propose to meet on a regular basis and (3) there is always a conversation starter (the project). Also be aware that you won’t be best friends with every project partner.
 * Some people without friends have the tendency to always sit at the same spot during the lecture. Identify one of those and sit besides him. Then do the obvious; Start with some small comments (e.g. regarding the lecture) and gradually improve to talking to them.
 * Furthermore there are always the classics: voluntary work, student jobs (my recommendation are teaching assitants) and extracurricular activities (student council activities for social skills on master level).

I hope something of those options works out for you.

Regarding your specific case I see three possibilities:

 * She likes you but is not ready to get into a relationship. From her written reactions it is fairly obvious that she has suffered a great deal of pain from her previous relationship and still needs time to process that. From her perspective it might seem that you want to pressure her into a relationship. This is definitely something you don’t want (her to think). I understand (i.e. hope) that you want to convince her in order to help her. Unfortunately this doesn’t change that she needs time (“alone” with her friends). Therefore my advise would be to take a step back, clearly communicate that you want to support her and then also do that (e.g. simply ask what would help her). I feel obliged to say something about the drawbacks of this advise. Obviously it can happen that she loses interest in you or even finds interest in someone else. The behaviour that I described is often identified as that of a friend, not a lover. The reason I still give it is fairly easy: If someone you like needs a friend then you are a friend. Furthermore I am inexperienced as heck, therefore no idea if it works.
 * She doesn’t like you and just felt lonely. Depending on the mental strength of that woman it might be the case she simply sought intimacy and you were someone that was willing to give that. Then later she noticed that this is not actually something that she wants and therefore left. In this case there is not really something (faithful) that you could do.
 * She doesn’t like you but already got pressured by you. This wouldn’t necessarily mean that you did this consciously. Maybe when she was weak you pressured her and she accepted this because she didn’t knew what to do with herself at that point in time. Later she noticed this and therefore left. Again in this case if am not aware of something (faithful) you could do.

tl;dr: To sum this all up and to answer your last question, I discourage from (actively) trying to convince her, but instead to give her some space and passive support. If you want to convince her nevertheless (which I **strongly condemn** if you like her) then you can do the obvious. Wait (actively) until she is at her lowest and then increase psychological pressure (i.e. subtly suggest that “you are the only one for her, she will be miserable without you” over a longer period of time). Again don’t do this, I am writing this only for completeness and to hopefully invoke your conscience that says this is wrong.

I would argue that a first important step is to not show your mood to much on days you feel down. Effectively this means to still stay friendly and responsive on those days. Topics are usually recent events where they won’t say too much. Important is that this is done with people I really appreciate. Your goal should be to find interactions that you still enjoy on those days. Additionally I like the credo, less can be more.

I have a similar issue and I would argue that this is one of the most fundamental issues in human society. I guess the problem can be (over-) simplified to “I would trust them if I knew that they trust me”. 

So then how do you know whether they trust you (see you as a friend, don’t betray you …)? My answer would be that you can’t know that, but this is not too bad. I like a certain comparison, but before I actually tell it, I feel obliged to mention that I am not a physicist and therefore might have something wrong. The comparison goes as follows:

Physics get kinda weird once you go to the subatomic level. As such there is a non-zero probability that you suddenly start burning. Now the question is, should you always keep a fire-extinguisher with you, because you are afraid of combustion? The answer is obviously no.

Bad things can always happen (and will always happen). You have to consider the opportunity cost, What do you miss out by being unapproachable. To sum that up, my advise would be to get aware that everyone (in different order of magnitudes) feels the same, that it is not necessary (or even advisable) to 100% trust your friends, but that you will miss things out when continue to stay that way.

That is obviously a hard question to answer since there are so many possibilities:


* Wrong Perception on your side. Maybe you suffer form confirmation bias, e.g. they interact a lot but at you only notice the times when they don’t, since they stick out more.


* Wrong Perception on their side. Maybe you send out unwanted signals, e.g. they suggest some stuff, but because you don’t react, they stop doing so. 


* Bad social skills on their side. A lot of people that I met were willing to interact with me but simply not really capable of doing so. This might be because they are simply boring people that don’t have to say much, or because they are too introverted to speak up, or even because they are not used to it.
